source.title: Increasing alignment of large language models with language processing in the human brain
source.authors: Changjiang Gao; Zhengwu Ma; Jiajun Chen; Ping Li; Shujian Huang; Jixing Li

record.tranche_reason: The study measures next-word prediction loss across language models of different sizes on its own reading stimuli, a different evaluation setup from the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports mean next-word prediction loss on 148 sentences and states that loss decreased with size for base models, while instruction-tuned models did not improve on these stimuli. Individual loss values are shown in a figure and referred to in supplementary tables that are not included in the supplied text. The paper's brain-alignment scaling results do not measure the loss, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream task performance named in the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Not a test. The study's question is model–brain and model–eye-movement alignment, built on the scaling premise and citing Kaplan et al. Its only loss result is a sanity check. It reports mean next-word-prediction (NWP) loss on 148 reading sentences for existing models from different families (GPT-2, LLaMA). These families differ in training data, tokenizer and architecture, so parameters are not isolated. Per-model values appear only in Fig. 2a and Supplementary Table 1, which is not supplied. The text says only that, for base models, loss decreased as size increased. A monotone qualitative trend over confounded families cannot show V1's power-law form, and the models were not trained as a controlled sweep. The headline 'scaling law' result concerns brain-alignment scores, a different construct from pretraining loss or downstream task performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that scaling LLMs from 774M to 65B improves alignment with human eye movements and fMRI, 'without any apparent diminishing returns', while instruction tuning does not. They report the base-model NWP-loss decrease only as a preliminary check. They also find that fine-tuned models' attention is more sensitive to instructions.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates NWP loss on 148 naturalistic reading sentences across existing model families; does not train model-size/data/compute sweeps or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported NWP-loss trend is stated for base models; instruction-tuned models did not improve NWP performance on the stimuli. No NWP-loss fit or sensitivity analysis is reported.

fits_no_version.finding: Alignment of attention matrices with regressive eye saccades and with fMRI rises with LLaMA size from 7B to 65B, plotted against log parameters. Instruction tuning gives no gain at matched size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model–brain/behaviour alignment scales with parameter count, roughly log-linearly, while instruction tuning does not change it.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean NWP loss on the reading stimuli decreases with size for base models, and instruction-tuned models do not lower it (Fig. 2a, Supp. Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across off-the-shelf base models, held-out loss on a small naturalistic text decreases monotonically with parameter count.

record.problems: For the NWP-loss result, the supplied text gives a qualitative trend but no numeric values or uncertainty; values are referred to in a supplementary table not included here. The evaluation uses only the study's 148 sentences and does not fit a power law.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant NWP-loss results left out. Brain-alignment results were not recorded as rows because they do not measure the loss or downstream task performance named in the claim versions.

untested.parts: Power-law form of loss vs parameters, tokens or compute. Only a qualitative monotone trend across confounded model families on 148 sentences is reported.
All. Brain-alignment scaling is not a training-loss regime.
All. The 13B Alpaca MMLU score is a single model check, not a scaling trend.

record.verdict_notes: Re-classified from 'tests'/T2 to uses_without_test, and the V1 'supports' label was removed. The loss evidence is qualitative, confounded across families, and has no readable values or fit. Fig. 2a appears to plot only GPT-2 774M among the GPT-2 models.

versions.untested_parts: Tests next-word prediction loss on the study's reading stimuli across model parameter sizes only; does not fit or establish a power law, test training-token or compute scaling, or establish behavior when other factors are not bottlenecks.
Small-run fits predicting much larger runs.
Compute-budget sweeps and the parameter/token allocation that minimizes loss.
Controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether a power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes; the study compares some base and instruction-tuned models but does not fit such laws.
Predictability of downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Sensitivity of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation to setup and fitting choices, or departures from a single power law.
